# The Longest Common Bitonic Subsequence: Match-Sensitive Algorithms and Conditional Hardness

**Abstract.** The longest common bitonic subsequence problem asks for a longest common subsequence of two ordered sequences whose values strictly increase and then strictly decrease; either phase may be empty. We formulate the problem through increasing and decreasing endpoint values at matching position pairs. This gives a constructive quadratic baseline and a match- sensitive algorithm based on two standard dominance-maximum passes. Its time is the sum of an input-sorting term and the number of matches times a squared logarithmic factor. We state the endpoint interface that permits reuse of increasing subsequence algorithms, and distinguish this specialization from new range searching machinery. A linear-size padding reduction transfers the conditional strongly subquadratic lower bound for longest common increasing subsequence to the bitonic problem. Reproducible implementations, exhaustive small-instance checks, and newly measured synthetic experiments document correctness and the practical tradeoff between sparse and dense processing.

**Keywords:** Longest common bitonic subsequence, longest common increasing subsequence, sparse dynamic programming, dominance queries, conditional lower bounds

## 1. Introduction

For two sequences _A_\[1_..n_\] and _B_\[1_..m_\] over a totally ordered alphabet, a common subsequence must respect the position order in both inputs. The longest common bitonic subsequence (LCBS) additionally requires a strict increase to one peak, followed by a strict decrease. Purely increasing and purely decreasing sequences are allowed. We write LCBS(_A,B_) for the optimum length, with value zero when the inputs have no common symbol.

The problem combines a simple value-shape constraint with two embedding orders. Let _V_={(_i,j_):_A_\[_i_\]=_B_\[_j_\]} and _M_=|_V_|. For a match _v_, let _I(v_) be the longest increasing common subsequence ending exactly at _v_, and let _D(v_) be the longest decreasing common subsequence starting exactly at _v_. The central identity is

\(LCBS(A,B)=max_{v\in V}\{I(v)+D(v)-1\},\) (1)

with the empty maximum interpreted as zero. Anchoring both halves at the same match makes their embeddings compatible; the peak is counted only once.

Our main algorithm evaluates these endpoint arrays using two sweeps over the matches and standard two-dimensional dominance maxima. Put _S=n+m_ and lg<sub>+</sub>_x_=log<sub>2</sub>(2+_x_). The resulting time bound is

\(O\big(Slg_+S+Mlg_+^2M\big),\) (2)

and total auxiliary space is _O(S+M_lg<sub>+</sub>_M_), including preprocessing. The dynamic-programming structure alone occupies _O(M_lg<sub>+</sub>_M_) space. These bounds include recovery of an optimal subsequence. The distinction between total workspace and the match structure matters when most input positions have no match.

### Contribution and scope.

The contribution is an explicit constructive treatment of the bitonic objective, together with a conditional hardness reduction. The sparse algorithm is a specialization of established dominance dynamic programming, not a new range-searching data structure. The dense algorithm is a baseline built from the usual longest common increasing subsequence (LCIS) scan. Equation (1) explains exactly which LCIS information must be retained: an endpoint value for every candidate common peak, rather than only a global optimum or one optimal increasing subsequence. Any LCIS algorithm exposing this interface can be substituted; we do not claim that existing LCIS algorithms are intrinsically unable to provide it.

Beyond this formulation, a padding construction gives an exact relation between LCIS and LCBS optimum values. Consequently, an \(O(N^{2-\varepsilon})\) algorithm for general length-_N_ LCBS inputs would contradict the known SETH-based LCIS lower bound \[1\]. This makes precise the worst-case limitation under which match-sensitive algorithms remain useful. The accompanying code independently validates the formulation and illustrates the crossover between the dense and sparse implementations.

#### Relation to the preprint.

An earlier version of this work is available as arXiv:2511.08958v2 \[2\]. That version already contains the two-pass dense and dominance-based algorithms. The present treatment consolidates their proofs and positioning, includes the formal padding reduction, and supplies a newly implemented and measured reproducibility package. The two algorithms are not claimed as additions relative to that preprint.

## 2. Related work and the endpoint interface

Classical longest common subsequence algorithms exploit either a dense position grid or the set of equality matches. Hunt and Szymanski \[3\] established the importance of the latter parameterization. The value constraints in LCIS and LCBS require information beyond the two position orders, but do not make the sparse viewpoint new.

Yang, Huang, and Chao \[4\] give a quadratic LCIS algorithm. Chan et al. \[5\] explicitly exploit the number of matching pairs. For two length-_N_ sequences, their LCIS bound is \(O(min\{Mlog\ell,N\ell+M\}loglogN+Sort(N))\), where \(\ell\) is the LCIS length, with logarithms conventionally bounded below by a constant. Kutz et al. \[6\] give an output-dependent expected bound in terms of LCIS length and alphabet size. These results are essential comparisons: match sensitivity and sparse LCIS processing predate the present formulation. Our \(Mlg_+^2M\) bound is not an improvement over the best LCIS bounds, and we do not claim it is the best achievable LCBS bound after adapting those algorithms.

**Proposition 2.1. (Endpoint lifting)**

Suppose an LCIS procedure reports the increasing endpoint length at every match of two sequences, with a predecessor match witnessing each nontrivial value. Two calls to that procedure, one on the original inputs and one on the reversed inputs, followed by _O(M_) work, solve LCBS and reconstruct an optimal subsequence. If _T_ and _W_ bound the time and workspace of each call, including endpoint reporting, the combined computation takes _O(T+S+M_) time and _O(W+S+M_) space.

#### Proof:

Reversal maps a decreasing suffix at (_i,j_) to an increasing prefix at (_n_+1-_i,m_+1-_j_) without changing values. Retain the first call’s _O(M_) endpoint records while making the second call. Select a peak by (1), and concatenate its two witnesses after removing one copy of the peak. The validity of this concatenation is proved in Lemma 3.1 below. Reversal, alignment by counting sort on match coordinates, scanning, and reconstruction cost _O(S+M_) additional time and space. \(\sqcap\sqcup\)

Proposition 2.1 is a two-pass reuse of LCIS with an explicit output requirement. A global LCIS length or one optimal witness does not supply the required per-match scores and immutable predecessor witnesses. Importing a faster LCIS bound requires accounting for these outputs in both calls; adaptive parameters such as the LCIS length may differ after reversal. Our direct dominance implementation makes these costs explicit.

For example, if both inputs equal \(\langle 9,8,7,6,1,2,3,4\rangle\), their LCIS and longest common decreasing subsequence lengths are four and five. Adding these global lengths and subtracting one gives eight, whereas LCBS has length five. The independently optimal halves cannot be joined at a common peak. Endpoint compatibility is therefore necessary even though its implementation uses familiar tools.

<tbc>Orthogonal range maxima and coordinate compression are standard techniques \[7\]. The implementation below uses nested Fenwick trees, extending the prefix-aggregation idea \[8\] to maximum values with witnesses. No improvement to these data structures is asserted. On the complexity side, Duraj, Künnemann, and Polak \[1\] rule out strongly subquadratic LCIS algorithms under SETH. This is compatible with logarithmic savings in the exponent-two regime, such as the LCIS algorithms of Duraj \[9\] and Agrawal and Gawrychowski \[10\]; strongly subquadratic means \(O(N^{2-\varepsilon})\) for a fixed \(\varepsilon>0\).

## 3. Match states and peak decomposition

A match _v_=(_i,j_) has value _a(v_)=_A_\[_i_\]=_B_\[_j_\]. Write \(u\prec v\) if both coordinates of _u_ are strictly smaller than the corresponding coordinates of _v_. A chain under \(\prec\) is an embedded common subsequence. The endpoint lengths satisfy

\(I(v)=1+max\{I(u):u\prec v,a(u)<a(v)\},\) (3)

\(D(v)=1+max\{D(w):v\prec w,a(w)<a(v)\},\) (4)

where maxima over empty sets are zero. Removing the last element of an increasing chain, or the first element of a decreasing chain, proves these recurrences in both directions. A witness attaining the maximum is retained as a predecessor or successor pointer; a singleton has a null pointer.

Figure 1 illustrates these states for \(A=\langle 2,1,3,4,6,5,4\rangle\) and \(B=\langle 1,2,3,5,6,4\rangle\). The highlighted witness \(\langle 1,3,5,4\rangle\) joins an increasing prefix of length three to a decreasing suffix of length two at the same match _v_=(6,4), giving _I(v_)+_D(v_)-1=4. **Lemma 3.1. (Common-peak decomposition)**
Equation (1) holds, and its maximizing match together with witnesses for (3) and (4) reconstructs an LCBS. **Proof:**
Fix an embedding of a nonempty bitonic common subsequence and let _v_ be its peak match. The prefix ending at _v_ has length at most _I(v_) and the suffix starting at _v_ has length at most _D(v_), so the full length is at most _I(v_)+_D(v_)-1. Conversely, concatenate optimum witnesses for these two states. Every nonpeak prefix match lies strictly before _v_ in both inputs, and every nonpeak suffix match lies strictly after _v_. Thus the embeddings do not conflict. The values strictly increase to _a(v_) and then strictly decrease, giving a feasible subsequence of the claimed length. Singleton and monotone witnesses are included. If _V_ is empty, only the empty subsequence is feasible. \(\sqcap\sqcup\) Pinters must identify a fixed match record, not a mutable column buffer. Following predecessor pointers strictly decreases both input positions; following successor pointers strictly increases them. Hence reconstruction terminates, visits exactly the reported number of elements, and costs time linear in the output length. Equal values may appear on opposite sides of the peak, but never as adjacent steps within a strict monotone half. ## 4. A constructive quadratic baseline The baseline adapts the LCIS row scan to report every match state. At the start of row _i_, _d[j_] is the maximum increasing endpoint length at column _j_ using rows smaller than _i_. The buffer _e[j_] identifies a fixed match attaining that value. Within the row, a running maximum records the best eligible earlier column with value smaller than _A[i_]. **Lemma 4.1.** Algorithm 1 reports all increasing endpoint lengths and valid immutable predecessor matches in _O(S+nm_) time and _O(S+M_) auxiliary space, including storage for the inputs’ reversed copies. For positive _n,m_, its scan takes \(\Theta(nm)\) time. **Proof:**
Before processing column _j_, _b_ is the maximum of _d[k_] over _k\

## 5. The match-sensitive algorithm

The dense scan touches nonmatching cells. We instead enumerate matches and compute (3)-(4) with dominance queries.

### 5.1. Preprocessing and the range-maximum structure

Assume comparison of two symbols and operations on an index take constant time. Sort the _S_ input occurrences by symbol, form equality groups, and assign ordered value ranks. Within each group, output all pairs consisting of an _A_ occurrence and a _B_ occurrence. This costs _O(S_lg<sub>+</sub>_S+M_) time and _O(S+M_) space. Matches can be stored in lists indexed by their _A_ row. All bounds below are deterministic in this comparison model.

Compress the columns occurring in a match to ranks \(x(v)\in[1..J]\); let _y(v_) be the symbol rank. For _M\>_0, \(J\le M\). Gaps in value ranks are harmless. Both order relations are preserved. A data structure _Q_ supports insertion of a scored match (_x,y,s,v_) and returns the maximum score and one witness in a prefix rectangle \([1..X]\times[1..Y]\). An empty rectangle returns \((0,\perp)\).

For completeness, an implementation with the stated bounds uses a Fenwick tree on the _J_ column ranks. Each outer node stores a sorted list of the value ranks of all points that can update it, and an inner Fenwick tree of maximum-score/witness pairs. These lists are built offline from the match coordinates. Each point appears in _O_(lg<sub>+</sub>_M_) lists; sorting them costs at most \(O(Mlg_+^2M)\) time and their total size is _O(M_lg<sub>+</sub>_M_). Binary search in each list locates an update coordinate or the last query coordinate at most _Y_ . Both operations visit _O_(lg<sub>+</sub>_M_) outer nodes and cost _O_(lg<sub>+</sub>_M_) per node. Only increases to stored maxima are needed. Ties may be resolved arbitrarily.

## 5.2. Two sweeps

In the forward sweep, process rows in increasing order and query (_x(v_)-1_,y(v_)-1) for each match _v_ in the current row. Add one to the returned maximum to obtain _I(v_). In the backward sweep, process rows in decreasing order and replace the column rank by \(\widehat{x}(v)=J+1-x(v)\). The query \((\widehat{x}(v)-1,y(v)-1)\) obtains the best decreasing successor. The value coordinate is not reversed.

**Theorem 5.1.** Algorithm 2 returns an LCBS in \(O(Slg_+S+Mlg_+^2M)\) time and _O(S+M_lg<sub>+</sub>_M_) auxiliary space.

**Proof:**

At the start of forward row _i_, _Q_ contains exactly the matches of smaller rows, with their correct increasing scores. The strict column and value bounds select precisely the remaining conditions in (3). Querying the whole row before inserting it preserves the invariant. By induction, all _I_ scores and predecessor witnesses are correct. In the backward sweep, stored matches have larger row indices. Mirroring makes a smaller query column equivalent to a larger original column. The unchanged strict<tbc>

value bound selects exactly the successors in (4). Thus all _D_ scores and successor witnesses are correct. Lemma 3.1 proves the returned result optimal. Preprocessing has the cost stated above. Offline structure construction and the two sweeps together take \(O(Mlg_+^2M)\) time. The final scan and reconstruction take _O(M_) time. Row lists, input ranks, and match records need _O(S+M_) space; one dominance structure needs _O(M_lg+_M_) space and can be released between sweeps. The _M_=0 case returns immediately after preprocessing and satisfies the same bound. \(\sqcap\sqcup\) ### Strictness and immediate updates. Row batching makes the index invariant explicit. Immediate updates within a row are also correct here: all matches in that row have the same value rank, and the query stops at _y(v_)-1, excluding every such update. This applies to both sweeps. It is a property of strict monotonicity; replacing the query bound by _y(v_) is incorrect even with batching, because equal- valued matches in different rows could then extend each other. For example, two identical constant sequences have LCBS length one. The supplied diagnostic implementation checks immediate and batched updates against the same independent oracle. ### When does the bound help? The sparse bound is asymptotically smaller than the dense bound when \(Slg_+S+Mlg_+^2M=o(nm)\). The sorting term must be included, particularly for unbalanced lengths. Merely assuming \(M\checkmark nm\) is not sufficient because each match incurs a logarithmic overhead. For dense inputs the simple scan can be faster and uses less auxiliary space. Neither the theorem nor the experiments assert universal superiority over the dense baseline or over potential adaptations of faster LCIS algorithms. ## 6. A conditional worst-case barrier The inclusion of increasing subsequences among bitonic ones does not alone reduce LCIS optimization to LCBS: a decreasing phase might improve the optimum. A fresh increasing suffix eliminates that possibility in an optimal solution. **Lemma 6.1. (Padding identity)**
Let \(Z=\langle z_1,\dots,z_K\rangle\) be strictly increasing, with all its symbols fresh and greater than every symbol occurring in _A_ or _B_. For \(K\ge 1\), \(LCBS(A\circ Z,B\circ Z)=max\{LCBS(A,B),LCIS(A,B)+K\}.\) (5) ### Proof: A common subsequence using no fresh symbol has length at most LCBS(_A,B_) when bitonic. A bitonic common subsequence using a fresh symbol must be purely increasing: original symbols precede all fresh symbols in both inputs, the transition to the fresh suffix is increasing, and fresh symbols appear in increasing order. A prior decrease would therefore be followed by an increase, while a later decrease is impossible. Its original part has length at most LCIS(_A,B_) and its fresh part has length at most _K_. Conversely, an original LCBS remains feasible, and appending all of _Z_ to an LCIS gives a

strictly increasing common subsequence of length LCIS(_A,B_)+_K_. These two constructions achieve both alternatives in the maximum. \(\sqcap\sqcup\) Choose _K_=min{_n,m_}+1. Since \(LCBS(A,B)\le min\{n,m\}\), the second alternative strictly dominates, and \(LCBS(A\circ Z,B\circ Z)=LCIS(A,B)+K.\) (6) The construction has linear size. Fresh symbols can be represented as tagged ordered symbols following the original alphabet. For integer inputs, a linear scan finds the maximum and the fresh symbols can be consecutive larger integers. Every optimal padded solution is increasing and contains all fresh symbols; otherwise a missing fresh symbol could be inserted. Removing the suffix therefore recovers an LCIS witness as well as its length. The construction adds exactly _K_ matches, since each new symbol occurs once in each input and matches no old symbol. **Corollary 6.2.** Assuming SETH, LCBS on two length-_N_ integer sequences has no \(O(N^{2-\varepsilon})\) algorithm for any fixed \(\varepsilon>0\). **Proof:**
Given two length-_N_ LCIS inputs, take _K=N_+1. Each padded input has length 2_N_+1. A strongly subquadratic LCBS algorithm, followed by subtracting _K_, would solve LCIS in strongly subquadratic time, contradicting the lower bound of Duraj et al. \[1\]. \(\sqcap\sqcup\) This is a worst-case, conditional statement for unrestricted inputs. It does not establish an unconditional quadratic lower bound, optimality of the logarithmic factors in Theorem 5.1, or hardness of every sparse regime. In particular, a bound depending on _M_ is consistent with the corollary because _M_ can be quadratic in _N_. ## 7. Reproducible implementation and experiments The accompanying supplement contains new Python implementations of the dense scan and the compressed two-dimensional Fenwick algorithm. Both recover match-coordinate witnesses and include preprocessing and reconstruction in their measured runtime. A third routine uses immediate strict updates as a diagnostic. No third-party Python packages are needed to run the algorithms, tests, or benchmarks. The measurements below were generated specifically for this revision; they do not reuse timings from earlier drafts. ### 7.1. Independent correctness checks An independent oracle enumerates all subsequences of the first input and tests their bitonicity and membership in the second input. Exhaustive testing covers all pairs of sequences of length zero through four over a three-symbol alphabet: 1212=14641 pairs. Another 1,000 seeded random pairs have lengths zero through eight and values from -3 through 4. For every pair, the tests compare the dense, batched sparse, and immediate sparse optimum lengths with the oracle, and check all reconstructed coordinates and values. They additionally compare every forward and backward endpoint

<tbc>score between the dense and sparse implementations and check the LCIS padding equality. All 15,641 test cases (14,641 exhaustive and 1,000 randomized) passed these checks. The validation log and test seeds are included. These finite tests check the implementation; the preceding proofs establish general correctness.

## 7.2. Measurement protocol

Inputs are independently uniform integer sequences over \(\{0,\dots,\sigma-1\}\), with _n=m=N_. Thus \(\mathbb{E}[M]=N^2/\sigma\). The density series fixes _N_=600 and varies the alphabet size; the scaling series sets \(\sigma=N\). Each configuration uses three independently seeded input pairs and three timed repetitions per pair and algorithm. Each algorithm is warmed up once before the series, and execution order alternates. Garbage collection runs before each timed call and remains enabled. Input generation and validation are outside the timed region. The clock is Python’s `perf\_counter\_ns`.

For each algorithm we first take the median of three repetitions on each input pair, then the median of those three medians.  1 reports these values, the median match count, and the ratio of aggregate dense time to aggregate sparse time. The ratio is calculated before rounding; it is not the median of individual speedups. All 180 raw timings, input-generation seeds, and the execution environment are included in the supplement. Each measured result was validated, and the two implementations agreed on optimum length for every benchmark input.

Measurements used CPython 3.12.14 on Windows 11 (build 26200), with an AMD Ryzen 7 5700X processor (8 cores, 16 logical processors) and approximately 32 GiB RAM. The algorithms execute sequentially in one Python process.

At _N_=600, the dense routine is faster for alphabet sizes 4, 16, and 64. The sparse routine becomes faster at the tested alphabet size 256, and its advantage grows as matches become rarer. The measured ratio ranges from approximately 0.21 at \(\sigma=4\) to 26.32 at \(\sigma=4096\). In the \(\sigma=N\) series it increases from 2.39 at _N_=200 to 11.19 at _N_=1600. These observations illustrate the cost of managing matches and the benefit of avoiding a full grid scan. They do not locate a universal crossover.

We have not implemented and validated LCBS adaptations of the adaptive LCIS methods of Chan et al. [5] and Kutz et al. [6], so the experiments compare only our two reference implementations. A like-for-like comparison through Proposition 2.1 must include both passes, per-match outputs, and reconstruction; timing an LCIS-only solver would measure a different task. This omission establishes no barrier to adaptation, and the results imply no superiority over those methods. The study also excludes optimized native implementations and peak-memory measurements; its single machine, synthetic inputs, and small seed sample do not support broad application claims. Python allocation, dictionary lookup, cache effects, and system load influence absolute times. Earlier application-oriented measurements are not used because their original scripts and logs were unavailable.

## 8. Conclusion

LCBS can be solved constructively by joining compatible increasing and decreasing endpoint states at a common match. Reporting these states is the precise interface needed to reuse LCIS techniques.

<tbc>A standard dominance implementation yields a transparent match-sensitive bound, while a simple padding identity transfers the SETH-based worst-case barrier from LCIS. The supplied implementation and fresh measurements document both sparse gains and dense overhead. Useful next questions are whether faster LCIS methods preserve all needed endpoint witnesses at their advertised cost, and how much reconstruction space can be saved without recomputing a large fraction of the states.
